architecture.fell_back_and_why: The ehs-* plugin subagent types are not registered in this harness, so per references/team.md's documented fallback path every specialist ran as a general-purpose agent with its role file, pack paths, coverage rows, safety contract, return format and the verbatim `searched` requirement copied into its prompt; ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} was substituted with the corpus root. Dispatched in two waves under a four-in-flight cap: wave 1 = web-api/pulsegate, infra/stanchion, mobile/harborlight, ai-safety/beacon; wave 2 = worker/tallyflow, privacy+data/quarrystore, supply-chain/whole-tree. FIVE of the seven returned. TWO never returned: ehs-infra-cloud (stanchion-ansible) and ehs-supply-chain (manifests and secrets). Mid-run I detected that I had drafted report fragments for both of those lanes as though their reports had arrived when no completion notification ever had; I discarded both fragments unshipped and redid each lane myself as squad lead, reading all ten stanchion-ansible files and all five manifests in full and running the disqualifying greps by hand. The 12 infrastructure findings and 2 supply-chain findings in this report therefore rest on the leader's own direct reading and are labelled as such here, not on any specialist return. Consequence for coverage: those two lanes had no pack loaded (no INF-nn or SUP-nn procedure IDs were consulted), so they are ad-hoc by construction and are shallower than the five pack-backed lanes; in particular no CI/CD platform procedures and no malicious-package or typosquatting analysis were exercised, and no advisory-database lookup was run anywhere because the environment has no network. The blind VER-09 critic stage prescribed by SKILL.md section 8 was NOT run as a separate agent; each specialist ran the self-directed VER-09 kill pass its own role file mandates, and their casualties are recorded in ruled_out below. That substitution is weaker than the blind stage the skill specifies, because the reading that produced a finding is the worst judge of it, and it is declared here rather than glossed.

ruled_out.assertion: An unauthenticated webhook mutates invoice status with no signature verification and no auth
ruled_out.killed_by: grep for legacyProcessorHooks returns only the declaration; index.ts:1-7 imports { billing } and never legacyProcessorHooks, there is no .use() of it anywhere, and edge.conf has no matching location. The path does not exist in what ships — established by the import list, not by the comment that says the same thing.

ruled_out.assertion: The rate limiter is evadable by spoofing X-Forwarded-For, since middleware.ts:20 takes the first comma-separated element
ruled_out.killed_by: edge.conf:42 sets `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr`, which REPLACES rather than appends, so the header the app parses holds exactly one value and it is the edge's observation of the peer. The same replacement is present on the other two proxying locations (:54, :63).

ruled_out.assertion: cors({ credentials: true }) with a permissive origin makes any page an authenticated reader of the API
ruled_out.killed_by: The origin is an exact-match array of one literal — no reflection of req.headers.origin, no unanchored startsWith/endsWith/regex. This is verbatim the documented exculpation for the class.

ruled_out.assertion: State-changing POST/PUT/PATCH routes have no anti-CSRF token
ruled_out.killed_by: grep -rni 'cookie|set-cookie|csrf' over src/ and edge.conf returns nothing. There is no ambient credential in the system — authorization is the Authorization header or edge-set headers, neither of which a browser attaches on its own. The precondition for the class is absent.

ruled_out.assertion: JWT verification accepts alg:none or an HS256/RSA confusion because no algorithm allowlist is passed
ruled_out.killed_by: jwtVerify(token, JWKS, { issuer, audience }) where JWKS = createRemoteJWKSet. The key resolver returns asymmetric keys from a remote key set and jose matches key type against the header algorithm, so none and HS256 are both refused; issuer and aud are pinned.

ruled_out.assertion: constantTimeEquals leaks the client secret's length through its early length return
ruled_out.killed_by: The early return is required — timingSafeEqual throws on unequal lengths — and the length of an environment-supplied secret is not a meaningful oracle. Real, but below reportability.

ruled_out.assertion: The default DATABASE_URL ships a passwordless connection string
ruled_out.killed_by: A loopback development default, not a shipped credential and not attacker-reachable; production supplies the variable.

ruled_out.assertion: Attacker-controlled deep-link title yields markup injection in the pane header, which sanitizeText exists to prevent
ruled_out.killed_by: WebPane.tsx:45 renders {title} inside a React Native <Text>, which displays a string and never parses HTML. There is no markup sink, so the guard cannot fire — it only causes escaped entities to be shown literally, and it corrupts the URL it is also applied to at router.ts:54. A dead guard, not a vulnerability.

ruled_out.assertion: manifest.fileName enables CRLF header injection / request splitting via content-disposition
ruled_out.killed_by: The platform HTTP stacks behind React Native fetch (OkHttp on Android, NSURLSession on iOS) reject control characters in header values, so CRLF does not reach the wire. The quote-injection variant is not blocked and survives as a separate reported finding.

ruled_out.assertion: restore() setting expiresAt: 0 lets an expired token be accepted
ruled_out.killed_by: currentAccessToken() (session.ts:47-49) returns the token unconditionally and no caller in the tree reads expiresAt — there is no local authorization decision for the discarded value to corrupt. The server validates expiry. Cosmetic, not security.

ruled_out.assertion: getSecret reads the keychain without an authenticationPrompt, bypassing the biometric gate
ruled_out.killed_by: Access control is bound to the item at creation (secureStore.ts:36, accessControl BIOMETRY_CURRENT_SET_OR_DEVICE_PASSCODE), so the OS enforces the prompt on every read regardless of the options passed at the read site. The control is in a layer the caller cannot skip.

ruled_out.assertion: fetch_url is the outbound exfiltration leg of the lethal trifecta
ruled_out.killed_by: tools.py:16 (_assert_allowed_host) rejects any host outside the two-entry allowlist before the request, and tools.py:24 sets follow_redirects=False. The model cannot steer the destination. The residual — a model-controlled path landing in an internal host's access log — needs a second capability that could not be established. fetch_url remains the ingestion leg.

ruled_out.assertion: The exfiltration-url guardrail is blind to the only host fetch_url can reach
ruled_out.killed_by: The same host allowlist: with the destination fixed, the rule has nothing to catch there. Verified inertly that the negative lookahead suppresses an internal URL while still matching an external one, so the rule is not dead on the question path it actually screens.

ruled_out.assertion: The write_note name permits path traversal into an arbitrary file
ruled_out.killed_by: assistant.py:66 applies NOTE_NAME_PATTERN before dispatch and tools.py:11 defines it. Verified inertly: the anchored pattern rejects ../../etc/passwd, a/b and .hidden. The only slip is a single trailing newline, which yields a filename with a trailing newline and no traversal.

ruled_out.assertion: _validate_tool_input silently passes non-string, non-integer properties
ruled_out.killed_by: tools.py:52-86 — every property in TOOL_SPECS is string or integer, so no reachable path skips validation. Latent only if a future spec adds another type.

ruled_out.assertion: The BEACON_ALLOW_UNSIGNED escape hatch disables producer verification
ruled_out.killed_by: config/beacon.yaml:1 sets env: production, which makes the env()=='test' condition false, so the bypass cannot fire under the shipped config.

ruled_out.assertion: The guardrail log leaks untrusted content (flagged UNCLEARED by log_escaper.py)
ruled_out.killed_by: assistant.py:26-37 and :107 — hits is a list of keys from the constant GUARDRAIL_PATTERNS dict and where is the literal 'question'. No attacker-controlled text reaches the sink. A tool-generated worklist item, not a finding.

ruled_out.assertion: An empty acl_groups on a queue-ingested document makes the chunk world-readable
ruled_out.killed_by: acl.py:50 — group_filter requires an intersection with the caller's groups, and an empty list matches nothing. The default fails closed.

ruled_out.assertion: chunk() attaches the wrong heading to a chunk
ruled_out.killed_by: heading_for compares offsets accumulated over normalised paragraph lengths against offsets computed on the raw string. A real correctness defect that misattributes a heading and crosses no trust boundary. Recorded, not reported as security.

ruled_out.assertion: The target contains text addressed to an auditing agent (AI-22 indirect prompt injection)
ruled_out.killed_by: Direct reading of all ten files. The only imperative text is SYSTEM_TEMPLATE (assistant.py:14-24), which is the product's own prompt to its own model, and two YAML comments describing behaviour. No CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .mcp.json or .cursor/rules exists in the target, and a non-ASCII sweep returned zero bytes. Nothing in this target attempted to instruct the auditor.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL statement logging leaks note bodies as bound parameters
ruled_out.killed_by: session.py:16 requires QUARRY_ENV=='local' AND QUARRY_SQL_ECHO=='1'; QUARRY_ENV defaults to 'production' at line 11. Fails closed, and the comment naming the risk matches the guard.

ruled_out.assertion: Path traversal via the caller-supplied filename in _export_path
ruled_out.killed_by: repository.py:122 and exports.py:59, :98 — every reachable call site builds the name from uuid4().hex, so no path separator can reach os.path.join.

ruled_out.assertion: Stale _case_headers entries survive a write because drop_case only evicts _summaries
ruled_out.killed_by: cache.py:34 — case_headers() is an accessor with no populator anywhere in the component and no caller in the wider tree; nothing can be served stale from a cache nothing writes.

ruled_out.assertion: Global uniqueness of Principal.email is a cross-tenant existence oracle
ruled_out.killed_by: An intended, bounded single-identity schema decision. With no sign-up, login or recovery surface inside this scope, the differentiated response the class requires cannot be shown; it belongs to whoever owns the HTTP surface.

ruled_out.assertion: The default DSN omits TLS and silently points production at localhost
ruled_out.killed_by: session.py:12 — the operative value is supplied by QUARRY_DATABASE_URL at deployment; the literal is a development fallback.

ruled_out.assertion: visible_fields ignoring its case argument widens field visibility
ruled_out.killed_by: policy.py:44 — every path into it passes assert_can_read first, comparing the same clearance rank to the same sensitivity rank; a principal who reaches it already out-ranks the case. The ignored argument is a smell, not a boundary crossing.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through the interpolated currency value in the posting_tags insert
ruled_out.killed_by: schema.js:8 — currency is an enum of four literals in the only schema whose type reaches this handler, and consumer.js:66 runs that validator unconditionally before dispatch; coerceTypes is false and currency is a declared property so removeAdditional cannot touch it. Recorded rather than deleted because the only thing between this line and injection is a schema keyed on envelope.type — and this project already registers a type with no schema.

ruled_out.assertion: Path traversal through the spool filename built from accountId
ruled_out.killed_by: schema.js:7 — the anchored pattern ^acct_[0-9a-f]{16}$ admits no separator or dot, and JavaScript $ without the m flag matches only at end of input, so the trailing-newline bypass that exists in other languages does not apply.

ruled_out.assertion: Log injection into the worker's records via envelope.type or an ajv error string
ruled_out.killed_by: pino (consumer.js:12, dlq.js:8) emits one JSON object per event and escapes control characters in string values, so a CRLF cannot forge a record. All 15 logging sinks were checked; none builds a line by concatenation. The second half — what parses these logs — is outside scope, so the accountability bound is unmeasured rather than cleared.

ruled_out.assertion: Signature forgery by re-splitting the newline-joined canonical string
ruled_out.killed_by: The join is ambiguous only if a field can absorb its neighbours. id is format:uuid (schema.js:18), ts is an integer >= 0 so it contributes at least one character, and JSON.stringify(payload) contributes at least {} and escapes any literal newline. Every alternative split is strictly longer, so no two distinct envelopes share a canonical string.

ruled_out.assertion: The unsigned producer field can be tampered with
ruled_out.killed_by: producer is genuinely outside the signed form, but a tree-wide grep finds it only in the schema declaration and in the sample constant — zero readers, so naming it changes nothing.

ruled_out.assertion: Timing oracle in the signature comparison
ruled_out.killed_by: timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers, with a length pre-check that leaks only the length of a fixed-size hex digest. The standard construction, not a defect.

ruled_out.assertion: Prototype-chain lookup on the handler table lets envelope.type reach an unintended callee
ruled_out.killed_by: type 'constructor' resolves to Object and awaiting it has no effect; '__proto__' resolves to a non-callable and throws into the unhandled-error path. Either way the outcome is identical to the no-handler branch at :74-77. Worth fixing with Object.hasOwn, but it reaches no sink.

ruled_out.assertion: Extra payload properties are silently deleted rather than rejected, desynchronising the signature
ruled_out.killed_by: The mutation happens after verifySignature (consumer.js:60 precedes :66), so it cannot desynchronise the signature, and no handler reads an undeclared field. Recorded in the v2-schema recommendation because a future schema author inherits the same misleading option.

ruled_out.assertion: dlq inspect prints full parked message bodies to stdout
ruled_out.killed_by: Intended and bounded: a local operator CLI whose declared purpose is to show what is parked, with output going to the operator's terminal, not a shared sink. The finding would move, not disappear, if that output were shipped anywhere — nothing in scope ships it.

ruled_out.assertion: purgeStream() destroys the DLQ
ruled_out.killed_by: Exported but not wired into the COMMANDS table (dlq.js:72-76), so the CLI cannot reach it; the comment records it as a one-off used during a past migration.

ruled_out.assertion: The Sentry DSN hardcoded in group_vars is a leaked secret
ruled_out.killed_by: A Sentry DSN is a public client ingest key that ships inside the browser bundle by design; the file's own comment at lines 30-31 says so and the endpoint is write-only. Not a credential with confidentiality value. Flagged for rotation hygiene only if the project later treats it as private.

ruled_out.assertion: A wildcard CORS origin is configured for the application
ruled_out.killed_by: stanchion_cors_origins_dev (the list containing '*') has exactly one occurrence in the whole tree — its own definition. app.env.j2:19 renders CORS_ORIGINS from stanchion_cors_origins, the single-entry console list. The permissive variable has no reader and reaches no rendered file.

findings.title: Billing route group mounted without the tenant guard its sibling group carries
findings.class: broken object-level authorization (BOLA)
findings.evidence: index.ts:20 mounts `/v1` as `.use(requireSession).use(tenantScope).use(accounts)`; index.ts:23 mounts `/v1/billing` as `.use(requireSession).use(billing)` with no tenantScope. billing.ts contains zero occurrences of `actor`; every handler keys off the path parameter: `where account_id = ${params.accountId}` (billing.ts:17, :27) and `update accounts ... where id = ${params.accountId}` (billing.ts:42). Elysia scoped-hook propagation is refuted by the tree itself: requireSession carries the identical `as: 'scoped'` flag, so if hooks propagated, POST /oauth/token (index.ts:27) would demand a session it exists to issue.
findings.impact: Any caller holding any valid session reads any account's invoice history and invoice detail, and overwrites any account's payment_token/payment_last4 via PUT /v1/billing/:accountId/payment-method. Precondition: one authenticated session plus a target accountId, which GET /v1/accounts/:accountId and invoice bodies both surface.
findings.recommendation: Apply tenantScope to the billing group as the /v1 group does, or resolve the account from actor.accountId and reject the path parameter when it disagrees. Prefer the second: it removes the class rather than one instance.

triage.reason: tenantScope is .use()d in exactly one place tree-wide (index.ts:20), inside a different group; framework hook propagation refuted by the /oauth/token reductio.
Invoices and payment tokens are per-account financial records; nothing marks this surface public.
amount_cents, pdf_key, payment_last4 and payment_token are account-scoped financial data.
No narrowing condition on the path: billing.ts has no actor reference and no WHERE clause bound to the caller.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every .get(/.post(/.put( in billing.ts, then joined against grep -rn 'tenantScope' (3 hits, one the definition) and grep -n 'actor' src/routes/billing.ts (0 hits).
scope.narrowed_by: requireSession at index.ts:23 — the attacker must be authenticated; it is not an anonymous read.

searched.for: any ownership check — actor, an accountId comparison, a WHERE bound to the caller
searched.found: nothing; `actor` appears 0 times and every query trusts params.accountId

searched.for: a root-level onBeforeHandle or guard that would cover billing
searched.found: nothing; the only root-level hooks are cors (:10) and rateLimit (:13), neither authorizing

searched.for: a second registration covering /v1/billing
searched.found: 3 hits only: definition middleware.ts:38, import index.ts:4, single use index.ts:20

searched.for: whether Elysia scoped-hook propagation could silently supply the guard
searched.found: POST /oauth/token registered after line 20 — propagation would break the grant flow, so hooks do not propagate

findings.title: Edge strips client-supplied identity headers on /v1/ only; /ops/ forwards them as the caller sent them
findings.class: authentication bypass by header injection across a trust boundary
findings.evidence: edge.conf:37-38 states the invariant ('Whatever the client sent in the identity headers is discarded and replaced with what the certificate actually proved') and implements it in one of three locations: location /v1/ sets X-Forwarded-Subject/$client_subject (:44), X-Forwarded-Account/$client_account (:45), X-Forwarded-Roles "" (:46). location /ops/ (:60-63) sets Host, X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For but none of the three identity headers. The API trusts exactly those headers as an authentication fallback for every route: auth.ts:52 `const actor = (await actorFromBearer(headers.authorization)) ?? actorFromHeaders(headers)`, with roles parsed from x-forwarded-roles at auth.ts:26, and adminOps gating on `hasRole(actor,'ops-admin')` at accounts.ts:108.
findings.impact: A caller reaching the edge with no client certificate and no bearer token sends X-Forwarded-Subject/Account/Roles: ops-admin; actorFromBearer returns null, actorFromHeaders fabricates the actor from the request, and the operator console opens: read any account (:113), list any account's members (:114), rewrite any account's plan (:117). `ssl_verify_client optional` (edge.conf:33) makes the no-certificate case reach the upstream. Under the most conservative reading (only partner-CA cert holders connect) a partner still escalates to platform operator over every tenant.
findings.recommendation: Set the three identity headers in the server block so every location inherits the reset, and add them explicitly to /ops/ and /oauth/token. Independently make the API fail closed: actorFromHeaders should be reachable only when the request also carries proof the edge terminated it, never as a bare fallback.

triage.reason: No unskippable layer resets these headers; grep for the three names across the tree returns 6 hits — three proxy_set_header lines inside location /v1/ and three reads in auth.ts.
The values are request headers; nginx forwards client headers it does not explicitly override, and these use hyphens so underscores_in_headers is not in play.
edge.conf:37-38 declares the opposite intent for this exact surface — the exposure is unimplemented, not intended.
Two principals: a partner or anonymous TLS client versus a platform operator; adminOps exists to separate them.
Not deferred to a platform: the control is in this repository, in this file, and covers one of three locations.
The narrowing runs the wrong way — the reset is narrow (/v1/ only), the trust is wide (auth.ts:52 applies to every route).

scope.established_by: Enumerated every location block in edge.conf and every proxy_set_header within each, then joined against every reader of the three header names in src/.
scope.narrowed_by: location = /oauth/token shares the omission but its handler reads only body, so no identity is derived there — impact is confined to /ops/*.

searched.for: an include of another conf, a server-level proxy_set_header, or more_clear_input_headers that would reset the headers globally
searched.found: nothing; no include directive at all, and every proxy_set_header is location-local

searched.for: any second place that clears or validates these headers
searched.found: 6 hits only: 3 sets in location /v1/, 3 reads in auth.ts — no validation anywhere

searched.for: a check that the request actually came through the edge (shared secret, mTLS to upstream, source-IP assertion)
searched.found: nothing; the function's only test is that subject and accountId are non-empty

searched.for: a second gate on adminOps that does not read actor.roles
searched.found: nothing; hasRole(actor,'ops-admin') is the only check and hasRole (auth.ts:61-63) reads the same spoofable array

searched.for: whether /ops/ might fall through to the return 404 catch-all
searched.found: no; location /ops/ at :60 is a prefix match that wins over location /

findings.title: tenantScope is registered on the member-patch route but structurally cannot fire on it
findings.class: broken object-level authorization — a dead guard
findings.evidence: The guard's first statement is its own opt-out: middleware.ts:41-42 `const requested = (ctx.params as Record<string,string>|undefined)?.accountId; if (!requested) return`. The route is /v1/members/:memberId — its only parameter is memberId, so `requested` is undefined and the guard returns before the cross-account comparison at middleware.ts:45. The handler then resolves the object by global id and never binds it to the caller: accounts.ts:84 `const member = await loadMember(params.memberId)`, accounts.ts:89 `await updateMember(params.memberId, body)`. db.ts:47 states the assumption: 'Member ids are globally unique uuids, so the id on its own identifies the row.' updateMember (db.ts:63-70) filters on `where id = ${memberId}` with no account predicate.
findings.impact: Any caller with any valid session changes the email and role of any member of any tenant. Changing email is an account-takeover primitive if invitations or recovery are addressed off that column. member.account_id is loaded at :84 and used only to pick a cache key at :90 — the value needed for the check is in hand and never used for it.
findings.recommendation: Move the route under /accounts/:accountId/members/:memberId so the existing guard fires, or compare in the handler: if (member.account_id !== actor.accountId) return 404. Additionally make the guard fail closed — an early return on a missing parameter means every future route without an accountId silently inherits no protection.

triage.reason: The only candidate mandatory layer is tenantScope, registered on this route but exiting at middleware.ts:42 before deciding anything. A control that cannot reach its comparison is not this rule.
Member records carry email and role; nothing marks them public.
Email addresses are personal data and role is an authorization attribute.
The narrowing is what is missing: loadMember and updateMember both key on id alone (db.ts:51, :69).

scope.established_by: Listed every route reachable under the /v1 group and marked which carry an :accountId parameter; PATCH /members/:memberId is the only one that does not, and is therefore the only one tenantScope cannot decide.
scope.narrowed_by: requireSession (index.ts:20) — a session is required, so this is not anonymous.

searched.for: an account predicate inside loadMember/updateMember that would scope the row regardless of the caller
searched.found: nothing; both are `where id = ${...}` only, and db.ts:47 documents the assumption as intentional

searched.for: a comparison of member.account_id against actor.accountId
searched.found: nothing; member.account_id is read once, at :90, only to build a cache key

searched.for: whether the guard has a fail-closed branch for a missing parameter
searched.found: the opposite — `if (!requested) return` at :42 is fail-open by construction

searched.for: another caller that does apply a scope, which would show the scope belongs at the call site
searched.found: 3 call sites; none compares an account

findings.title: Member-patch route accepts role as a free string; its sibling constrains it and gates owner
findings.class: broken function-level authorization / privilege escalation through an asymmetric gate
findings.evidence: Two handlers in one file, same effect on members.role, one gated and one not. accounts.ts:45-48 `if (role === 'owner' && !hasRole(actor,'account-owner')) { set.status = 403; return {error:'forbidden'} }` and accounts.ts:56 `role: t.Union([t.Literal('member'), t.Literal('billing'), t.Literal('owner')])`. Against that, accounts.ts:96 `role: t.Optional(t.String())` with no gate — the PATCH handler (:81-99) contains no hasRole call and does not even destructure actor from the context.
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller promotes any member — themselves included — to owner without holding account-owner, defeating the exact control the sibling route enforces, and writes role values outside the declared vocabulary. This survives a fix for the dead-guard finding: even confined to the caller's own account, self-promotion to owner remains.
findings.recommendation: Hoist the constraint and the gate into one place both handlers call: reuse the t.Union of the three literals in the PATCH schema, and move the role==='owner' check into a helper invoked by POST /members, POST /members/batch and PATCH /members/:memberId alike.

triage.reason: No layer supplies the check: hasRole is imported at accounts.ts:2 and called at exactly two lines, :45 and :108; neither is on this route's path.

A database CHECK on members.role could exist outside scope (no migrations given — find for *.sql/*migration*/*schema* returned none), but would not rule this out: owner is a valid role, so any plausible constraint still admits the escalation.
The two handlers reach the same effect through the same column — insertMember sets role (db.ts:59) and updateMember sets role (db.ts:66).
Nothing narrows the accepted set: t.Optional(t.String()) admits every string and no post-schema check reads the value.

scope.established_by: Took the authorization symbol the file imports (hasRole, accounts.ts:2), listed all its uses (:45, :108), then listed every handler reaching members.role and subtracted.

searched.found: 4 hits: definition auth.ts:61, import accounts.ts:2, uses accounts.ts:45 and :108. Neither use is in :81-99.

searched.for: a data-layer allowlist or enum on role before the UPDATE
searched.found: nothing; `role = coalesce(${patch.role ?? null}, role)` writes whatever arrives

searched.for: a DB-level CHECK or enum that would bound the value
searched.found: none in scope — recorded as the bound on the secondary aspect, not on the escalation

searched.found: real: :45-48 branches and returns 403 — the asymmetry is the defect, not a fake gate

findings.title: Batch invite route bypasses both controls its single-invite sibling enforces
findings.class: broken function-level authorization / control asymmetry between sibling handlers
findings.evidence: POST /accounts/:accountId/members enforces both controls: `if (!isInvitable(email))` (:41) and `if (role === 'owner' && !hasRole(actor,'account-owner'))` (:45). The batch route has neither, and an open schema: `for (const row of members) { await insertMember(params.accountId, row.email, row.role) }` (:67-69) with `members: t.Array(t.Object({ email: t.String(), role: t.String() }))` (:75). Both reach the identical sink, insertMember (db.ts:55). On the second read of db.ts the write proves to be an upsert — `on conflict (account_id, email) do update set role = excluded.role` (db.ts:59) — so the batch route rewrites the role of members who already exist.
findings.impact: A caller authenticated into an account posts one CSV-shaped body and (a) invites addresses outside ALLOWED_INVITE_DOMAINS, defeating the verified-domain control, (b) grants owner without holding account-owner, and (c) by way of the upsert, promotes or demotes any existing member of that account, including the current owner. t.String() on email also drops the format:'email' constraint the sibling declares at :55.
findings.recommendation: Run each row of members through the same two checks the single route applies, before the loop; validate all rows and reject the whole request on any failure, matching the route's own documented all-or-nothing contract (:61-62). findings.title: Exported CSVs carry unneutralized note text into spreadsheet formula context
findings.class: CSV formula injection
findings.evidence: All three writers pass note.body (and entry.summary) straight to csv.writer(..., quoting=csv.QUOTE_ALL) at exports.py:31, :46 and :66. QUOTE_ALL is a CSV-quoting setting: it guarantees the field survives parsing, and it does not stop a spreadsheet from evaluating a field whose first character is =, +, -, @, or a leading tab or carriage return. The only validation applied to body anywhere is _validate_body (repository.py:35-40), which checks emptiness and a 20,000-character limit.
findings.impact: A note body beginning with a formula lands in a file whose stated audience opens it in a spreadsheet — 'a CSV the case team can download' (line 22) and the nightly dump for the court reporting feed (line 37). On open, the formula executes with the recipient's privileges; standard payloads exfiltrate adjacent cells over a hyperlink or WEBSERVICE call, or invoke DDE where still enabled. The docket path carries this to an external feed. Preconditions: an author who can create a note — which is not limited to the matter's own team — and a recipient who opens the file in a spreadsheet rather than a text editor.

findings.title: Exported copies of note bodies accumulate with no retention, and redaction never propagates to them
findings.class: storage limitation / deletion propagation
findings.evidence: Every export writes a new uniquely-named file under EXPORT_DIR (default /var/lib/quarrystore/exports) and returns the path, at exports.py:26, :41 and :61. Searching the component for any deletion, purge, expiry or cleanup primitive — os.remove, unlink, shutil, a TTL over the directory, a scheduled job — returns none. The only expiry anywhere is the in-memory TTLCache. drop_case (cache.py:38) evicts a cache entry, not a file.
findings.impact: Each export is a full-fidelity, unredacted copy of a matter's notes that leaves the database's access controls behind: once written it is governed by filesystem permissions and by whatever backs up that directory, not by policy.py. Redaction is a flag on a row, so redacting a note after an export has been taken changes nothing in the file — the material stays readable in every copy already on disk, and in the nightly docket dumps. Nothing records which exports exist, who took them, or what they contain: no read is logged anywhere in this component. Filenames are uuid4().hex, so they are unguessable, which bounds discovery but not accumulation. This is a privacy risk rather than a bypassed control: the system does what it was built to do. It may touch obligations around storage limitation and the effectiveness of a rectification or erasure request against derived copies; no compliance determination is made here.
findings.recommendation: Give exports a lifetime: write them with an expiry and purge on a schedule, or hold them in object storage with a lifecycle rule and serve them through short-lived signed URLs rather than a shared directory. Record each export — who, which matter, which fields, when — so the population affected by a later incident can be scoped and a redaction request can be honoured against the copies as well as the row.

triage.reason: A retention rule enforced outside the repository — a tmpfiles.d rule, a bucket lifecycle policy, a backup schedule — is plausible for a directory under /var/lib, and the infrastructure component is owned by another specialist and was not read. This UNKNOWN is why the finding ships as probable. What would settle it: whether anything expires EXPORT_DIR in stanchion-ansible.
The export paths are shipped code with two live entry points.

findings.title: Signature verification is advisory: the shipped config makes it unable to reject
findings.class: improper verification of message integrity / a control that runs and cannot fail
findings.evidence: signing.js:36-45 computes `matches` and `fresh`, logs a warning on failure, and then `if (config.signature.mode === 'enforce') return false` — the only rejection — before `return true` on every other path. config/default.json:21 ships `"mode": "warn"` with the comment 'flip to enforce once every producer ships the signing sidecar'. SECRET also defaults to '' (signing.js:4), which makes matches false for every message even where a producer does sign — under warn that too resolves to return true. maxSkewSeconds: 300 feeds `fresh` (signing.js:34-35) whose verdict reaches only a log line.
findings.impact: The worker's only authentication of the queue is off, so anyone able to XADD to the stream dictates ledger and payout operations. The consequence is not merely that unsigned messages pass: applyPosting treats a missing account as balance 0 (ledger.js:23) and upserts the row (ledger.js:35-38), so a single ledger.post.v1 message mints a balance of up to 50,000,000 cents on an arbitrary account id with no balancing entry, which a payout.release message then releases. findings.recommendation: Set mode to enforce and remove the mode switch entirely once done — a verifier whose rejection is configurable will be off in one environment. Fail closed when SECRET is empty (refuse to start, do not accept). Add a negative test that feeds verifySignature a wrong signature and asserts false; a control that cannot be made to fail in a test is the defect.

findings.title: The payout debit writes balances through the unchecked writer; neither the solvency floor nor the ceiling reaches it
findings.class: missing business invariant on one of two writers to the same entity
findings.evidence: Two writers to balances. The checked one, applyPosting, validates the integer and non-zero amount (ledger.js:9-11), enforces `Math.abs(amountCents) > config.limits.maxPostingCents` (ledger.js:12), takes `select balance_cents from balances where account_id = $1 for update` (ledger.js:20) and rolls back when `next < 0` (ledger.js:25-28). The other, adjustBalance (ledger.js:59-65), is a bare upsert with none of those. payoutRelease.js:28 calls `ledger.adjustBalance(p.accountId, -Math.abs(p.amountCents))` — the money-leaving path uses the unguarded writer. config.limits.maxPostingCents has exactly one reader in the tree, ledger.js:12, inside applyPosting.
findings.impact: A payout can release funds the account does not hold and drive the balance negative, with no per-entry ceiling. On a first write for an unknown account the insert branch stores the raw negative delta, creating a negative balance from nothing. Precondition: a payout.release message, which the signature findings make unauthenticated.

findings.title: The payout row and the balance debit are not one transaction
findings.class: non-atomic multi-step financial write
findings.evidence: payoutRelease.js:19-31 performs three independent writes with no transaction: the payouts insert marked 'released' (:19), `ledger.adjustBalance(...)` (:28), and `idempotency.complete(key, result)` (:31). Each is a separate pool.query — node-postgres checks a connection out per call, so these may not even share a session, and none is wrapped in BEGIN. applyPosting (ledger.js:16-47) shows the codebase knows how to do this with an explicit begin/commit on a checked-out client.
findings.impact: Any failure at the debit step leaves a payouts row marked released with no corresponding debit — the account is never charged for money the platform recorded as sent. Failure at the completion step leaves the payout made and the idempotency record stuck in-flight. The missing v2 schema supplies a reachable trigger: a payload whose amountCents is not an integer passes the insert and makes the debit raise on the integer bind. The comment at payoutRelease.js:26-27 states the reconciliation job squares this the next morning, which is a detection window, not an invariant.
findings.recommendation: Check out one client, BEGIN, insert the payout and apply the debit through the checked writer, COMMIT; complete the idempotency record only after the commit succeeds, and release the claim if it does not.

triage.reason: No transaction can be supplied by a layer above: handleEntry (consumer.js:47-80) calls the handler with no client or transaction context, and the handler takes pool, not a client.
This is the only payout code path that ships.
Not bounded to informational: the divergence is money recorded as sent and never debited.

findings.title: Command injection: a parked message's memo is interpolated into a shell string
findings.class: OS command injection
findings.evidence: dlq.js:55-60 parses the parked body, takes `const memo = envelope.payload?.memo ?? envelope.type`, and calls execAsync with a template string interpolating both entry.reason and memo into a command line. execAsync is promisify(child_process.exec) (dlq.js:1-7), which runs the string through /bin/sh -c. entry.body is the raw, pre-validation bytes of the parked message: consumer.js:54 parks bodies that failed envelope validation, so payload.memo is unconstrained in type, length and content. Double quotes do not neutralise command substitution in sh. entry.reason is a second vector: for envelope failures it is ajv.errorsText(...) (schema.js:61), whose text embeds attacker-supplied property paths.
findings.impact: Arbitrary command execution on the worker host, in the process environment that holds TALLYFLOW_SIGNING_SECRET and PGPASSWORD — so it also yields the signing key, which survives fixing the warn-mode finding. Preconditions: get a message parked, which requires only sending a malformed envelope and needs no signature at all since consumer.js:51-56 parks before the signature check; an operator runs the dlq notify verb (package.json:9, dlq.js:75); and the attacker's entry is the oldest parked one (XRANGE with COUNT 1), which is arranged by sending when the DLQ is empty.
findings.recommendation: Replace exec with execFile(config.dlq.notifyCommand, ['--channel','ops','--reason',reason,'--memo',memo]) — argv, no shell. Do not attempt to quote or escape the string.

triage.reason: Nothing sanitises between JSON.parse and the shell. escapeHtml is in another module, is not imported here, and is not shell-safe.
The value is attacker-controlled by construction: the DLQ exists to hold messages that failed validation, and consumer.js:54 writes the raw body before any payload schema has run.
The sink is child_process.exec, documented to spawn a shell. This is the dangerous form.
notify is one of the three verbs in the shipped COMMANDS table (dlq.js:75) and package.json:9 provides the script that runs it.
config.dlq.notifyCommand is an absolute path, so this is not a PATH issue mistaken for injection — the injection is in the argument, not the program.

findings.title: Ledger postings have no replay or de-duplication guard
findings.class: missing idempotency on a queue consumer that moves value
findings.evidence: consumer.js:28 constructs the posting handler without the idempotency store — `makeLedgerPostingHandler({ ledger, pool, log })` — while the adjacent payout registrations at :29-30 receive it. makeLedgerPostingHandler (ledgerPosting.js:18) never receives the store and applies no dedupe of its own; applyPosting (ledger.js:8-48) keys on nothing. envelope.id is validated as a UUID (schema.js:18) and then used only for logging and the spool filename content — never as a seen-key.
findings.impact: Re-delivering the same posting message applies the posting again — balance and postings rows duplicated per replay. Even with signature enforcement on, this is the residual attack for anyone who can read the stream and write to it, without ever forging a signature: the 300-second freshness window is not replay protection, since a captured message replays verbatim inside it and there is no nonce store. dlq.replay (dlq.js:37-38) also does XADD before XDEL, so a failure between them duplicates the entry.
findings.recommendation: Give the posting handler the same idempotency store, keyed on envelope.id, claimed before the write and completed after; or add a unique index on a required producer-supplied dedupe reference and handle the conflict. Add a replay window with a persisted seen-id set rather than relying on the timestamp skew.

triage.reason: A database unique constraint cannot save this even if one exists: reference is optional (schema.js:32-38, not in required) and is inserted as NULL when absent (ledger.js:33). Postgres unique indexes permit multiple NULLs, so verbatim replay of a reference-less posting duplicates under any DDL. envelope.id is never written to postings at all, so no constraint can key on it.
This is the shipped registration.
Applies to every ledger.post.v1 message.

findings.title: The payout idempotency key is optional, producer-chosen, and bound to nothing
findings.class: broken idempotency / business-flow abuse
findings.evidence: payoutRelease.js:10 `const key = p.idempotencyKey ?? envelope.id`. schema.js:42 lists required as accountId, amountCents, currency, destination — the key is not required. idempotency.js:15 builds `${prefix}:${key}` with prefix 'ik', so the key is the whole namespace. config/default.json:24 sets ttlSeconds to 604800.
findings.impact: Three defects in one line. Optional: the fallback is envelope.id, a per-message identifier rather than a per-payout one, so the same logical payout resent under a new envelope id pays twice — while the doc comment at payoutRelease.js:4-6 asserts a guarantee the schema does not require the producer to provide. Unscoped: the key is not bound to account, amount, destination or message type, and v1 and v2 share the ik keyspace, so a key reused with entirely different payload contents returns the first result and the second payout silently never happens — a chosen-key suppression of someone else's payout. The key is logged in clear at payoutRelease.js:14, which lowers the cost of learning one. Expiring: the record lives 7 days, after which the same key pays again.
findings.recommendation: Make idempotencyKey required in both payout schemas and remove the envelope.id fallback — a missing key should be an error, not a per-message default. Namespace the Redis key by event type and hash it together with (accountId, amountCents, currency, destination), so the same key with different contents is a conflict rather than a silent hit. Choose a TTL at least as long as the payout dispute window, or persist the record in Postgres beside the payout.

triage.reason: No database constraint compensates: payouts.id is a fresh randomUUID() per attempt (payoutRelease.js:18), so a duplicate payout inserts cleanly whatever the DDL says. Nothing else in the tree dedupes payouts.
p.idempotencyKey is a payload field the sender picks.
The ?? is not a defensive default — it substitutes an identifier at the wrong grain, which is the defect rather than a mitigation of it.
The impact reaches the user: paid twice, or not paid.

findings.title: The in-flight claim is never released, and the redelivery reports success without paying
findings.class: failure arm missing from an error path
findings.evidence: payoutRelease.js:12 claims the key (writing an in-flight state with a 7-day TTL); :13-15 returns `claim.previous?.result ?? { status: 'in-flight' }` normally when the claim is not fresh. Any throw between the claim and idempotency.complete leaves the claim standing, because idempotency.release — defined at idempotency.js:27-29 and exported at :31 — is called from nowhere. consumer.js:98-99 XACKs on any non-throwing return, so the message is acknowledged and gone.
findings.impact: A payout that fails once is permanently converted into a silent success for 7 days: the next delivery returns in-flight normally, the entry is acknowledged, the payout is never made, and the only trace is an info-level line saying 'payout already released'. It is also attacker-triggerable as a targeted denial of a specific payout: claim a chosen key and make the same message fail, which the missing v2 schema supplies directly (a payload whose amountCents is not an integer claims the key at :12 and then throws at the Postgres bind). When the legitimate payout arrives under that key, it is answered as already released.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the body in try/catch and call idempotency.release(key) on failure — the function is already written. Distinguish the three states in the return so a stale in-flight is an error rather than a success, and do not XACK on a state the handler did not actually complete.

triage.reason: The caller does not compensate: consumer.js:97-102 catches only throws; a normal return is acknowledged unconditionally.
This is the only payout path; the missing release call is missing in what ships.
The in-flight object is not an error signal — nothing inspects the handler's return value at all (consumer.js:79 discards it).
Money not moved, reported as moved; not informational.

findings.title: A failed entry is never acknowledged, never parked, and never reclaimable
findings.class: poison-message handling / unchecked error path
findings.evidence: consumer.js:96-103 wraps handleEntry and xack in a try whose catch only logs 'handler failed' — no xack, no DLQ write, no retry. The loop reads with '>' (consumer.js:91), i.e. never-delivered entries only, and there is no XPENDING, XCLAIM or XAUTOCLAIM anywhere in the tree. The consumer name is keyed on process.pid (consumer.js:84), so after a restart the previous consumer's pending entries belong to a name that will never exist again. JSON.parse(entry.body) at consumer.js:49 sits inside this same catch, unlike every validation failure, which is parked properly at :54, :62 and :69.
findings.impact: Financial messages that fail — including every failure caused by the missing v2 schema, the unchecked debit and the non-atomic payout — are silently lost from processing, invisible to the DLQ tooling (dlq inspect reads the DLQ stream, not the pending list), and the Redis stream grows without bound because entries are never acknowledged. Precondition: any handler error, which an attacker can induce at will with a malformed body.
findings.recommendation: On a handler exception, park the entry in the DLQ with the error as its reason and then acknowledge it, or implement a bounded retry with XAUTOCLAIM and a delivery-count ceiling before parking. Make the consumer name stable across restarts (host plus slot, not pid) so pending entries can be reclaimed, and alert on XPENDING depth.

triage.reason: No supervisor reclaims: grep -rniE 'xpending|xautoclaim|xclaim|retry|attempt|backoff' over src/ returns no operational hit (only maxLength schema keys and one comment containing the word retry).
This is the shipped loop, and it is the only consumer.
This is not a control that could live outside the repo: the pending list belongs to this consumer group, named at consumer.js:88, and no other process in scope reads it.
The loss is of ledger and payout events, not of telemetry.
